explanations.explanation: That's the very first thing out of the LORD's mouth: “Shout for joy, O barren woman, who bears no children; break forth in song and cry aloud…” Notice He doesn't say "hold it together." He says CRY ALOUD. I think that's a woman who just got permission to be as loud as she wants.

I get why you'd go there, since the woman has never had a child. But the LORD tells her to cry aloud in a different way: “break forth in song and cry aloud…” The loud part is right. The sad part isn't in His words. He says shout for joy.

Quiet waiting sounds so polite, friend. But the LORD isn't asking for polite here. He says, “Shout for joy, O barren woman…” and “break forth in song and cry aloud.” That's not a whisper. That's a woman with the windows open.

Yes, and that's the surprising part. The LORD says “more are the children of the desolate woman than of her who has a husband.” You'd expect the numbers to go the other way. I think that's why it lands so hard.

I understand the doubt, because it sounds backwards. But the text says it's the desolate woman who has more children. The LORD says “more are the children of the desolate woman than of her who has a husband.” The woman nobody expected to have a house full is the one who gets it.

Yes, ma'am, and bigger is the whole assignment. The LORD says, “Enlarge the site of your tent, stretch out the curtains of your dwellings, do not hold back.” Then He adds, “Lengthen your ropes and drive your stakes in deep.” That's a woman being told to stop being modest about her floor plan.
Packing a tent away means you're done with it. The LORD says the opposite. He says, “Enlarge the site of your tent…” and “do not hold back.” The tent stays up, and it gets bigger.

Patching is a good tent habit, I'll give you that. But the LORD never mentions holes. He says to stretch the curtains, lengthen the ropes and drive the stakes in deep. Nobody's reaching for a repair kit in this verse.

explanations.answer: She will spread out right and left
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the LORD gives: “For you will spread out to the right and left…” Her descendants will also “dispossess the nations and inhabit the desolate cities.” So the tent grows because the family does. That's a lot of folding chairs.

explanations.answer: A great storm is coming her way
explanations.explanation: A storm is a fair guess when somebody's told to drive stakes in deep. But the LORD doesn't mention a storm here. The reason He gives is, “For you will spread out to the right and left…” The extra room is for growing.

explanations.answer: Her old tent will soon fall apart
explanations.explanation: That makes sense on paper. But the LORD says nothing about her old tent falling apart. His reason is that she “will spread out to the right and left,” and her descendants will take over the desolate cities. The tent grows to fit the future.

I see why you'd think so, since shame can feel permanent. But the LORD says the opposite. He says, “you will forget the shame of your youth and will remember no more the reproach of your widowhood.” That shame doesn't get a lifetime lease.

Right, she won't carry it. The LORD says, “For you will forget the shame of your youth and will remember no more the reproach of your widowhood.” Forget it. Remember it no more. I think that's one heavy bag finally set down.
Her Maker! The LORD says, “For your husband is your Maker—the LORD of Hosts is His name…” The very One who made her is the One who stands by her. I did NOT see that coming the first time, friend.
A prince sounds like a solid catch. But the LORD doesn't name any human at all. He says, “For your husband is your Maker…” Her husband is far bigger than a prince.

A king of Persia is a very fancy guess. But the text never puts a king anywhere near this wedding. The LORD says, “For your husband is your Maker—the LORD of Hosts is His name…” That's a husband no throne can top.
Deserted is the word. The LORD says, “like a wife deserted and wounded in spirit, like the rejected wife of one's youth.” It's a hurting picture. And He's the One saying He has called her back.

Cherished is a lovely word, but it's the wrong end of the story. The LORD says she's like “a wife deserted and wounded in spirit.” A wounded spirit doesn't sound cherished. That's exactly the one He calls back.

Nobody's throwing a party for this wife yet. The LORD says she's like “a wife deserted and wounded in spirit, like the rejected wife of one's youth.” Celebrated isn't in it. The calling back is where things turn.

A brief moment. The LORD says, “For a brief moment I forsook you, but with great compassion I will bring you back.” Compare that to the great compassion coming after. It's a small moment next to a big promise.
Seventy years is a specific number, and it's not here. The LORD says, “For a brief moment I forsook you…” Brief is the word He picks, and then He says He will bring her back with great compassion.
A lifetime feels long enough to cover how it hurts. But the LORD says, “For a brief moment I forsook you…” Then He turns to “everlasting kindness.” The moment is short and the kindness isn't.

I can see how the "moment" talk could trip you up. The moment is about how long He hid His face. His kindness is a different thing. He says, “In a surge of anger I hid My face from you for a moment, but with everlasting kindness I will have compassion on you.”

Right, because the moment belongs to the hiding. The LORD says, “In a surge of anger I hid My face from you for a moment, but with everlasting kindness I will have compassion on you.” Everlasting means everlasting. That's the one that sticks around.

explanations.answer: The waters would never again cover the earth
explanations.explanation: That's the oath. The LORD says, “I swore that the waters of Noah would never again cover the earth.” Noah is the man who went into the ark with his family (Genesis 7:7). Then He says He has sworn the same kind of thing to her: He will not be angry with her or rebuke her.

explanations.answer: Rain would never again fall on the earth
explanations.explanation: That would make for some dry gardens, friend. The oath is about the flood, not about rain. The LORD says He swore “that the waters of Noah would never again cover the earth.” Noah is the man who went into the ark (Genesis 7:7).

explanations.answer: Every mountain would be made low forever
explanations.explanation: Mountains do show up in this passage, but not in Noah's oath. The oath is that “the waters of Noah would never again cover the earth.” Mountains come two verses later, where they may be removed but His loving devotion will not depart. Noah is the man who went into the ark (Genesis 7:7).

True, and He puts it in the strongest picture around. He says, “Though the mountains may be removed and the hills may be shaken, My loving devotion will not depart from you, and My covenant of peace will not be broken.” Mountains move before His covenant of peace does.

I get why you'd hesitate after all that talk of anger and hiding. But the LORD says it plainly: “My covenant of peace will not be broken.” He says it even if the mountains are removed and the hills are shaken. It's rock solid, and I mean sturdier than rock.

Yes! Stones set in antimony, foundations of sapphires, pinnacles of rubies, gates of sparkling jewels, “and all your walls of precious stones.” Not one thing in this build is ordinary. Somebody's getting the nicest address in the whole book.

Cedar and gold sound fancy, but the LORD picks something else. He says, “I will set your stones in antimony and lay your foundations with sapphires.” Then come rubies, sparkling jewels and precious stones. Jewels are the whole building material.

Bronze and iron are what you'd expect for a city. But the LORD never mentions them. He says her gates will be “sparkling jewels,” and “all your walls of precious stones.” This city is built out of treasure.

I see why "only a few" could sound right when you picture a small, hurting city. But the text says all of them. The LORD says, “Then all your sons will be taught by the LORD, and great will be their prosperity.” No one gets left out of the classroom.
That's it. The LORD says, “Then all your sons will be taught by the LORD…” All, not some. And He adds, “great will be their prosperity.”

explanations.answer: It will not come near her
explanations.explanation: That's what He says: “Terror will be far removed, for it will not come near you.” Right before that He says, “you will have no fear.” Terror doesn't even get close enough to knock.

explanations.answer: It will come back one day
explanations.explanation: I know that's how worry likes to work, friend. But the LORD says, “Terror will be far removed, for it will not come near you.” He doesn't leave a return date. It doesn't come near her at all.

explanations.answer: It will camp outside her walls
explanations.explanation: Camping outside sounds close enough to make you nervous. The text says it's “far removed.” The LORD says, “for it will not come near you.” No tent, no lawn chair, no parking spot.
Yes, they fall. The LORD says, “If anyone attacks you, it is not from Me; whoever assails you will fall before you.” Whoever comes at her ends up on the ground in front of her.

Her gates are sparkling jewels, so I get the temptation. But the LORD says the one who attacks is the one who loses. He says, “whoever assails you will fall before you.” Nobody walks off with the gates.

explanations.answer: They will make peace with her
explanations.explanation: Peace would be a nice ending, but that's not what He says here. The LORD says, “whoever assails you will fall before you.” The attacker is the one who falls.

True. The LORD says, “Behold, I have created the craftsman who fans the coals into flame and forges a weapon fit for its task.” He made the one at the forge. I think that's one of the biggest things in the passage to chew on.

It can feel strange, but the text is plain. The LORD says, “Behold, I have created the craftsman who fans the coals into flame and forges a weapon fit for its task.” He's the One who created him. That's what the verse says.
Right. The LORD says, “No weapon formed against you shall prosper…” The weapon can be made, but it doesn't win. And He goes on to say she will refute every tongue that accuses her.
Melting is a pretty picture, but it isn't what the text says. The LORD says, “No weapon formed against you shall prosper…” The weapon gets formed. It just doesn't get anywhere.

explanations.answer: It will be handed to her
explanations.explanation: Nobody's handing out weapons in this verse. The LORD says, “No weapon formed against you shall prosper…” The weapon is formed against her, and it doesn't prosper.

Yes. He says, “This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD, and their vindication is from Me,” declares the LORD. The safe city, the jewels and the weapons that can't win all belong to His servants.
Kings are the usual guess for who gets a jeweled city. But the LORD says, “This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD…” His servants are who it belongs to.

Noah did come up earlier in the passage, so I see why he's stuck in your head. But the LORD ends with, “This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD…” It belongs to His servants. That's the line He wraps the whole passage in.
That's right. He says, “their vindication is from Me,” declares the LORD. It doesn't come from their strength or their name. It comes from Him, and you can't hand that job to anybody else.
Strength is what we usually lean on, friend. But the LORD says, “their vindication is from Me.” It isn't something they make for themselves. It comes from Him.
A good name is worth a lot, but the LORD doesn't say it's the source. He says, “their vindication is from Me,” declares the LORD. That means it comes from Him.
